strengths: Clear motivation addressing a genuine problem in text-to-image prompt engineering: existing LLM-based prompt expanders often prioritize style/aesthetics at the expense of user semantic fidelity.
The proposed framework is training-free and plug-and-play, integrating Davidsonian Scene Graph (DSG) decomposition with VLM verification to identify and expand only the missing concepts.
Extensive empirical experiments across three diffusion backbones of varying generations (SD v1.5, SD v2.1, and Flux-dev) across multiple benchmark subsets.
Human preference evaluations (Fig. 4) provide corroborating evidence that the refined prompts improve both semantic consistency and aesthetic quality over original prompts.
weaknesses: Severe risk of circularity in evaluation: VisualPrompter uses DSG question decomposition and Qwen2-VL verification as its core optimization signal, and the main quantitative evaluations (DSG-1k and TIFA v1.0 in Tables 1 & 2) use the exact same DSG decomposition and Qwen2-VL answering metric. This inherently biases quantitative results in favor of the proposed method.

Absence of comparable iterative/feedback baselines: The evaluated baselines (Promptist, NeuroPrompts, BeautifulPrompt) are feed-forward single-pass prompt generators that do not observe the generated image. The paper lacks comparison against standard multimodal iterative refinement baselines, such as prompting an MLLM (e.g., GPT-4o or Qwen2-VL) directly with the initial image and prompt to self-correct the text.

High inference latency and resource overhead: VisualPrompter requires an initial image generation pass, LLM DSG parsing, multi-question VLM inference, LLM concept expansion and prompt composition, followed by a second image generation pass. The computational cost, latency, and token overhead are not measured or reported.

Aesthetic enhancement relies largely on naive keyword appending (Prompt Decoration), which achieves modest improvements on aesthetic metrics (Table 4) unless coupled with external tools like NeuroPrompts (which then deteriorates semantic consistency).

strengths: Intuitive closed-loop framework: Using visual feedback via a vision-language model (VLM) to diagnose missing concepts in generated images and iteratively refine text-to-image (T2I) prompts is well-motivated and conceptually sound.

Training-free and model-agnostic design: VisualPrompter does not require fine-tuning diffusion backbones or prompt-rewriting LLMs, making it easily applicable to different generative backbones (e.g., SD v1.5, SD v2.1, and Flux-dev).
Paper presentation and clarity: The manuscript is generally well-structured, easy to follow, and supported by informative diagrams and visual examples.
weaknesses: Severe circularity and evaluation bias: The framework uses Qwen2 as the LLM and Qwen2-VL as the visual evaluator to construct DSG questions, identify failed concepts, and guide prompt rewrite. Crucially, Section 4.3 uses the exact same Qwen2-VL model and DSG evaluation protocol to measure semantic accuracy. Optimizing prompts specifically to satisfy Qwen2-VL's responses on DSG questions and then measuring success with Qwen2-VL on DSG creates a direct optimization-against-the-metric leak. An independent evaluation with distinct VLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, or LLaVA-OneVision) or human annotations on unseen compositional benchmarks is necessary to validate real improvements.

Limited technical novelty: The core workflow is an orchestration of existing off-the-shelf components—Davidsonian Scene Graph (DSG) parsing, binary VQA with a pre-trained VLM, and prompt expansion via prompting an LLM, followed by appending common heuristic aesthetic tokens. The algorithmic contribution beyond assembling these existing tools is relatively thin.

Unaddressed computational and latency overhead: Generating an initial image, decomposing it via LLM, performing multi-query VLM inference for every atomic concept, running two LLM generation passes (expansion + composer), and regenerating the image adds immense inference latency and compute cost. The paper lacks runtime, FLOPs, and API/token cost analyses, and fails to compare VisualPrompter against standard test-time compute alternatives such as Best-of-N sampling or standard re-ranking.

Weak and narrow baseline selection: The compared baselines (NeuroPrompts, Promptist, BeautifulPrompt) are primarily single-turn prompt rewriting or aesthetic modifier methods from 2022–2023. The paper lacks comparisons against modern multimodal feedback/self-correction loops (e.g., direct multimodal LLM critique/refinement, visual programming/reflection pipelines, or iterative diffusion steering).

strengths: Clear problem identification: The paper correctly identifies a critical flaw in many existing T2I prompt engineering frameworks—namely, that optimizing purely for visual aesthetics often leads to concept omission and semantic drift from user intent.

Modular and training-free design: VisualPrompter leverages off-the-shelf LLMs and VLMs without requiring expensive fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, making it straightforward to apply across diverse diffusion models (demonstrated on SD 1.5, SD 2.1, and Flux-dev).

Principled fine-grained concept targeting: Utilizing Davidsonian Scene Graphs (DSG) to decompose prompts into verifiable atomic concepts enables targeted concept enrichment rather than uncontrolled whole-prompt rewriting.

Solid ablations: The ablation study (Table 5) effectively isolates the contributions of visual feedback versus open-loop refinement, as well as DSG-guided concept expansion versus direct LLM rewriting.
weaknesses: Severe evaluation circularity / Metric bias: VisualPrompter employs DSG decomposition and Qwen2-VL in its SERE loop to detect missing concepts and refine prompts, while the primary evaluation metric (Section 4.1–4.3) also evaluates text-image consistency by running Qwen2-VL VQA on DSG representations. Optimizing directly against the evaluation representation and model family introduces significant evaluation bias; cross-evaluating with independent MLLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) or alternative vision-language benchmarks is necessary.

Unfair baseline comparison: VisualPrompter operates in an iterative, closed-loop fashion (Generate $\rightarrow$ Inspect with VLM $\rightarrow$ Refine $\rightarrow$ Regenerate), whereas all compared baselines (Promptist, NeuroPrompts, BeautifulPrompt) are single-turn, open-loop text enhancers that never observe generated visual outputs. More suitable baselines should include test-time visual feedback alternatives, such as VLM-based best-of-$N$ / rejection sampling and general iterative multi-modal prompt refinement without DSG.

Substantial computational overhead and latency: Executing two full diffusion generation passes, an LLM parsing step, multi-question VLM visual question-answering passes, and an LLM re-composition step incurs a high inference latency and memory footprint. The paper lacks quantitative discussions or profiling of runtime, token usage, and inference cost compared to standard pipelines.

Underwhelming aesthetic performance: In Table 4, VisualPrompter achieves noticeably lower Aesthetic Scores than existing prompt engineering methods. When the authors integrate an aesthetic keyword booster (NeuroPrompts), they observe a substantial decline in semantic consistency, revealing that the core tension between prompt aesthetics and prompt fidelity remains largely unresolved.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: existing text-to-image prompt engineering techniques frequently optimize for visual aesthetics at the expense of prompt-image semantic alignment, leading to significant degradation in semantic faithfulness.

The proposed atomic semantic-level approach (leveraging Davidsonian Scene Graphs to identify and expand only missing concepts) is principled and transparent compared to unconstrained end-to-end LLM prompt expansion.
Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple state-of-the-art generative models (SD 1.5, SD 2.1, Flux-dev, Janus-Pro) on standard alignment benchmarks (DSG-1k and TIFA v1.0).

Thorough evaluation setup, including human preference studies, ablation experiments, and a cross-VLM validation (using Llama-3.2-Vision) to address potential evaluator bias arising from using Qwen2-VL in the loop.
weaknesses: Inference latency and computational cost: VisualPrompter requires a full generation pass, LLM parsing, VLM visual question answering, LLM expansion, and a second image generation pass. While Table 6 reports total latency, the requirement of running both an LLM and a VLM alongside the diffusion model significantly limits real-time usability.

Limited novelty of individual components: The framework largely orchestrates existing methodologies (DSG generation via LLM, VQA via VLM, prompt expansion via few-shot prompting, and aesthetic keyword concatenation) into a sequential pipeline without new learning algorithms or novel model architectures.

Single-turn feedback limitation: The method operates purely in a one-step reflection-and-regeneration manner. The paper does not analyze whether multi-round reflection cycles improve accuracy or cause semantic drift and prompt bloating.

Missing comparisons with visual-feedback self-correction methods: Comparisons are primarily restricted to text-to-text prompt optimizers (Promptist, NeuroPrompts, BeautifulPrompt); the paper lacks empirical comparisons with existing visual-critique / self-correcting diffusion frameworks (e.g., Self-correcting LLM-controlled diffusion models).

strengths: The paper is clearly structured and easy to follow, providing comprehensive implementation details, prompts, and templates in the supplementary material.
Extensive experiments are conducted across multiple generative backends (Stable Diffusion v1.5/v2.1, FLUX-dev, Janus-Pro) and benchmarks (DSG-1k, TIFA v1.0).
The motivation to move beyond superficial aesthetic prompt expansion toward semantic faithfulness and missing concept identification is reasonable and relevant.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline selection: The method utilizes an iterative visual-feedback loop (generating an image, probing it with a VLM, rewriting via an LLM, and regenerating). However, the baselines compared against (NeuroPrompts, Promptist, BeautifulPrompt) are purely single-turn, text-only prompt expanders primarily designed for aesthetic styling. The paper omits comparisons against prior visual-feedback or self-correcting T2I methods (such as Wu et al., CVPR 2024, 'Self-correcting LLM-controlled Diffusion Models', or other closed-loop VLM-guided refinement systems).

Methodological novelty is limited: The framework primarily orchestrates off-the-shelf tools and existing paradigms without fundamental algorithmic innovation. Generating question graphs via LLMs comes directly from DSG (Cho et al., 2024), question answering is done by standard VLMs (Qwen2-VL), and prompt rewriting/decorating is done via standard few-shot prompt templates.

Evaluation circularity / metric contamination: VisualPrompter explicitly detects which DSG questions are answered negatively on the initial image and instructs the LLM to rewrite the prompt to pass those exact DSG concepts. Evaluating the resulting output primarily on DSG/TIFA question-answering accuracy creates a circular setup where the method is directly optimized to satisfy the evaluation test queries.

Aesthetic evaluation is weak: As shown in Table 4, the proposed method alone trails the aesthetic baselines. The paper has to append NeuroPrompts to match baseline aesthetic performance, which in turn degrades semantic consistency.

Incomplete ablations regarding VLM interaction: The ablation compares DSG-based expansion against direct Qwen expansion without feedback, but does not isolate the necessity of the complex DSG tuple-graph pipeline against a straightforward direct visual conversational critique baseline (e.g., asking a VLM directly 'What elements of this prompt are missing in the image, and how should the prompt be refined?').

strengths: Addresses an important and practical limitation of existing T2I prompt engineering frameworks: prior prompt optimizers typically focus on aesthetics and styles at the expense of semantic fidelity and user intent.

The proposed closed-loop pipeline (DSG-based concept decomposition -> VLM visual verification -> target-specific expansion -> LLM prompt reconstruction) is intuitive, training-free, and model-agnostic.

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse generative backbones, including older diffusion models (SD 1.5, SD 2.1), state-of-the-art flow/diffusion models (Flux-dev), and autoregressive multimodal models (Janus-Pro).

Good experimental diligence: the authors perform human evaluation (user study), ablation on individual modules, check for evaluator bias using an independent VLM (Llama-3.2-Vision in Appendix L), and analyze latency overhead.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison (closed-loop vs. open-loop): The selected baselines (Promptist, NeuroPrompts, BeautifulPrompt) are purely text-based, feed-forward prompt expanders that never inspect the generated image. Comparing an iterative visual-feedback system to single-pass text expanders gives VisualPrompter an inherent information advantage. Comparisons with visual feedback/self-correction frameworks (e.g., Wu et al., CVPR 2024; or LLM-guided iterative image editing/reprompting) would provide a fairer assessment.

Metric alignment circularity: The optimization process explicitly decomposes prompts into Davidsonian Scene Graph (DSG) atomic tuples and refines them to answer DSG questions affirmatively, while the primary evaluation metric is itself accuracy on DSG / TIFA question answering. This raises the question of whether the prompt is merely being overfitted to pass VLM-as-a-judge QA checks rather than fundamentally improving semantic generation on neutral benchmarks (e.g., GenEval).

Ad-hoc aesthetic decorator: While the semantic reflection module is structured, the aesthetic enhancement step relies on appending generic keyword templates (e.g., '4k, highly detailed, elegant'), which is quite primitive and results in lower aesthetic scores compared to methods like NeuroPrompts (Table 4).

Computational latency and cost: Running an initial T2I generation, an LLM parser, a VLM question-answering step over multiple atomic concepts, an LLM rewrite, and a second T2I generation significantly increases end-to-end latency (nearly doubling FLUX generation time to ~34s), which limits deployment in real-time interactive settings.
